Interviewer:	So I’ll tell you a bit about the project – I’m looking at women in engineering, and about influences on people that are about to go on industrial placement and we are interviewing some people that aren’t going on placement as a comparison really. So we’re looking at why women decided to do engineering in the first place and a bit about their experiences so far, in education and then what they expect to get out of the placement. And we’re hoping to improve women’s retention, in the engineering industry. So that’s what it’s all about. So I’m going to start asking you some background questions and why you wanted to go into engineering. But is your course, materials with management? 

Subject:	Yes 

Interviewer:	OK. What A levels did you do?

Subject:	Geology, Chemistry, Maths and I did an ‘AS’ in RE.

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	I went to a Church of England secondary school and then just like a sixth form college.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	Er, in the industry?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	I’ve had random jobs in the local butchers but that’s it.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine – what do your parents do? Are either of them in the industry at all?

Subject:	No, my mum’s a – well, they’re both teachers. My mum’s head of the maths department at a secondary school and my dad, a teacher at a college, doing woodwork and other stuff like that.

Interviewer:	OK, I keep talking about engineering but you’re not actually in the engineering department, are you? So do you consider what you’re doing is engineering?

Subject:	Well, it’s in the title so I assume it is engineering, but yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, just thought I’d check because we are also interviewing design and technology students (lost words).

Subject:	Well, we’re IPTME, so yeah, Institute of Materials, Technology 

Interviewer:	Polymer’s in there somewhere as well isn’t it?

Subject:	Yeah Polymers, Technology, Materials and Engineering. So, I’ve always thought of it as being engineering.

Interviewer:	Yes, that’s OK. So when and why did you decide to do this?

Subject:	It was completely random. Erm, no actually I was thinking of doing engineering, of some description anyway, because of my ‘A’ levels. Something scientific but I didn’t want to do chemistry, so I thought right, what can I do? You know. First of all I thought like doing – like chemical engineering, but when I looked into it, it’s not actually anything to do with chemistry much at all. It’s like sort of architecture really – so it sounded more like building plants and I just thought no that sounds horrendous. And then I happened to be wandering past the stalls for materials engineering, when I came round to look round Loughborough – to look at like the chemical engineering. And I picked one of them up and I thought oh I could do this actually. It looks quite interesting, so I ended up doing it.

Interviewer:	OK, when you chose your ‘A’ levels, had you thought about what you wanted to do, more long term?

Subject:	Well, at the time I was thinking of doing a – I don’t know – I thought, at one point, I was gonna do something like food – micro biology and I’ve been going to do all kinds of things. I’ve always like thought it would be vaguely scientific but beyond that I’ve never been sure exactly what I wanted to do.

Interviewer:	OK, did you have much careers advice at school?

Subject:	It was useless at school to be honest. We had – I think – I don’t know, we just had something in – like in the final year, you know we did like some practice interviews and wrote a CV, and had to think of your attributes thing. 

Interviewer:	But no information like, this is what engineering is?

Subject:	No, we didn’t get any like actual things like that, till we were in college, when we were choosing what degree we wanted to do. Even then we were pretty much in the dark, you kind of decided yourself what you wanted to do and then looked into things on your own.

Interviewer:	Did you do much research into careers then?

Subject:	Yeah, well one of the reasons I chose materials, was because it said that they need more people in it and I thought, well if they need more people, then I’m more likely to get a job at the end of it. There’s no point spending 3 years of my life learning about something you find is useless.

Interviewer:	Yes. Have your family been quite supportive of you?

Subject:	Yeah, well my mum just thinks it’s hilarious because like, in my house I’m really like known for not being the brightest of sparks. I’m a bit – I’m a bit busy. Like I’ve been – I had to go on a random trip for [company] once, and I had to sit on a bus for like an hour because I’d left my (?) like – I had to go to the end of line to pick it up (oh no). My mum says – I was on the phone one day telling her what I’d been doing, she said, what are you doing girl, because I’m not – I don’t think I’m really an engineer, to be honest.

Interviewer:	OK, what, what is it do you think that appeals to about the course that you’re doing?

Subject:	Er, it doesn’t – a lot of the time, but now I’m doing it, I’m sort of stuck with it. ‘Cos talking to other people, they don’t like their courses either. Too much learning for the sake of learning and they’re just rubbish, but in reality you just look it up in a book, if you wanted to learn certain facts and figures but I like – I do like some of the modules. A lot of it depends on the lecturer. If you’ve got a good lecturer, anything can be interesting can’t it? But the actual - I do quite like the actual materials, but you’re learning about different packages and stuff.

Interviewer:	Is the course not what you expected it to be?

Subject:	I thought it had been what I was quite expecting really. You know, learning anything’s a bit of bore. Once you know the information it’s kind of more interesting, it’s just learning it in the first place that’s a bit of a chore.

Interviewer:	What would you say are some of the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	I like – I quite like the labs actually. It’s a lot of work for what they’re worth – the lab and parts and stuff. So I do quite like actually doing them.

Interviewer:	Is that more hands-on stuff then?

Subject:	Yeah, well we just break things. Break in the machines and break in one way or another.

Interviewer:	Are there many girls on the course?

Subject:	Well, strictly speaking, like managing materials and management are the only sides of it anyway. Let’s go on – if we just go on materials then there’s 3 girls but if you have – put all of them together then there’s – automotove materials as well, then that dilutes us down a bit because there’s like 30 of them and 3 are girls. (OK) But now, in 2nd year we share a lot of our modules with DT students and that anyway. We’ve got the odd extra girl from there. It doesn’t bother me, I get on better with males anyway.

Interviewer:	OK, did you expect it to be so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah, it just – it just – it’s bound to be, isn’t it, because of the way the brain works, I’ve seen programmes about it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	No, not particularly. If they want to do it, then they’ll do it regardless. If they don’t want to do it then there’s no point trying to force them to do something, if they don’t want to do it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women are provided with the information about engineering, to be able to make like a decision whether to do it?

Subject:	Well to be honest nobody’s really provided with much information – I found that, anyway. I was pretty much left to my own devices. I suppose they could – they could make it more, but there quite a lot of schemes and things going on, trying to encourage women into it, but at the end of the day, if they want to – if something else appeals to them – they can go off and do human biology or whatever it is they fancy doing…

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that the reason why women don’t do more engineering type subjects is based on false perceptions of what engineering is?

Subject:	Er, I don’t know – most people I know just chose their course because they – it just appealed to them because of the subjects they’d done previously. It’s only an extension of them, the one’s that they enjoyed. So it just depends, but I suppose as well, a lot of it – it probably – it’s the physics because well, in my course I didn’t need to have physics, I got in on the fact that I did chemistry and maths but a lot of the other engineers – because you need physics and not that many girls do physics at ‘A’ level (yeah) so they haven’t the right ‘A’ levels to start with.

Interviewer:	So if you did want to encourage more women into engineering, you’d have to start before that?

Subject:	Yeah, you have to start with ‘A’ levels and in getting them to do Physics at A level. Actually they tried to make me do it, and I was like, I don’t think so.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	You’re supposed to be analytical and have – you’ve got to be good at like turning things round in your mind and I think it’s spatial awareness and there’s dimensions and things.

Interviewer:	Do you think that those characteristics are more male than female?

Subject:	Well, they’re supposed to be according to studies and stuff.

Interviewer:	And do you think that…?

Subject:	I don’t know because I do find – I’ve been doing these psychometric testings for my placement – and I, and I found the English one a complete doddle – I’ve always been good at English and I’ve been good at maths but – I’m good with numbers but not necessarily engineering. I can do the numbers but not mechanics itself – I haven’t really and studied much - I can’t actually look at things and know what’s going to happen? Maybe I would if I did study it a bit more but I don’t have to, and as far as I’m concerned that’s good.

Interviewer:	So do you think that men have a tendency to do better in that then?

Subject:	I think, a lot of them – well I know my friend [name] who’s on the course, he kind of likes tinkering about with his bike and stuff anyway but I think that’s a male thing to do, you know when a girl’s handed a doll and the boy’s handed a mechano set.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any advantages to being a woman in such a male dominated environment?

Subject:	Possibly, but you have to be careful ‘cos you’re doing – possibly it would be easier to get your own way. Women are better at manipulating people than males but having said that you want to – you want to get where you get by the fact that you work, you know the best anyway. I don’t suppose it really makes that much of a difference (OK) although having said that, my sister is applying for (? sciences?) – I don’t know if it works the same – but they were saying with her being, she’s a tiny little blonde thing, so her being – looking like she does, they said she needs to be loads better than everybody else because they’re not gonna take her seriously otherwise. Which, I suppose, that could be a problem. But, me not being quite such a tiny blonde thing, I don’t suppose I’d have those problems.

Interviewer:	OK, we’ve talked a bit about the course so far, have you been taught by female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yes, oh actually one of my best lecturers is a – [name] – she’s brilliant – she’s absolutely – I’d say she’s probably the best out of them.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s anything to do with her being a woman?

Subject:	Erm, no I think it’s to do with her just being really dedicated to what she does, and she just – and I think, I think as well, with her being younger she is more aware of the fact that she keeps people interested. She’s really good at getting the balance between giving you enough information so that you’re not having to continually be writing and not taking any of it in, but, at the same time not – you haven’t got it all sat there, to switch off. She’s good at keeping everyone involved and she’s also like really well prepared and stuff. Erm, yeah, and she’s – but we’ve got – well, [name] we have – she’s useless, she really is. She’s urgh – you just go in and you just don’t want to be there. She’s not very good delivering.

Interviewer:	Do you notice any differences in say the types of subjects that the female lecturers are teaching or their styles of teaching?

Subject:	She’s erm, [name] did thermo-dynamics, but then that’s what she does, ‘cos she’s only just become a professor so I went to her inaugral lecture, and she does the mathematical models of – I think it’s a (coon?) or something like that. I don’t know, I started to fall asleep a bit. It was really wild at the time but it was – something very mathsy anyway. I suppose technically that’s more what you would have thought of as being male than any other thing. I don’t know really.

Interviewer:	Do you find it encouraging that you’ve got female lecturers? Or would you find it encouraging if you had more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, I guess it is encouraging that – yeah, that she’s there – I don’t tend to think that much about it, to be honest. Just kind of accept the way that things are and I mean, I went into it, knowing that it was going to be male dominated and that just doesn’t bother me, because I kind of assumed that nowadays it wouldn’t make any difference when I do work a job, whether I’m male, female, you know, whatever, since there’s all different laws and stuff.

Interviewer:	Do you think that she has done quite well to get there – Professor [name]?

Subject:	Yeah, she’s the youngest – she’s the youngest one to get one I think.

Interviewer:	Youngest female or…?

Subject:	I think so – I’m not sure if she’s the youngest or not, I thought she said the youngest ‘cos she’s pretty young anyway, but maybe she deserved it, so fair enough.

Interviewer:	Do you see her as a role model at all?

Subject:	Well no, well yes, sort of, in that I suppose she’s good for proving what you can achieve if you set your mind to it, but I don’t want to do that anyway – I don’t want to stay in academia, because I just don’t fancy that. I want to go into actual industry maybe or I might even not do engineering at all – I might manage something. I don’t know, I haven’t decided.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, there’s not really – there’s not that much actual interaction between the lecturers and the students anyway, sort of turn up, sit there, get talked at and go away again. I mean, I’m actually - with my department being a lot smaller, most of them I think, they would actually know who I was, or recognise me because in the first year, we had a course social and there was me and the 2 guys that I went with. And all the other lecturers and your – like research students and stuff, so they’d all know who I was, even though I wouldn’t necessarily know them. But, erm I’m our course rep as well, so I’m on like the staff/student committee so them lot know me really well anyway. I don’t think, I suppose erm, like [name] the technician’s always nice to me because I’m female more than he’ll speak to the males I guess. Well, it starts off as female but it’s more the fact that, they feel like they have to look after you more but generally because that’s the way I play it with them, because then you get what you want more, it’s not necessarily, so if you want to use the machine, instead of waiting 6 hours, you can wait less. But the actual lecturers - there’s not really any difference because you don’t really have that much interaction.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Male or female?

Subject:	He’s male.

Interviewer:	Are you bothered that they’re male would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	No, erm, I’m fine with a male ‘cos he’s (OK) – I mean I don’t – I’d never go and see him for anything anyway. If there’s ever a problem with me, I tend to keep it to myself. I like tell my best friends. Well, I had a massive like crisis after the awfulness of my (?) stupid, poxy test that I’ve – well it was actually like crying on my friend’s shoulder, saying oh right, what we gonna do? And went to the careers service and sorted it out myself. I don’t generally go to sort of tutors or whatever, anyway.
Interviewer:	OK. If that’s how you prefer to deal with it…? 

Subject:	Yes, at the time I prefer to deal with it anyway. I don’t think, if it was a woman, I don’t think I’d feel any more inclined to go and see them.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine. Is there anyone that’s been the biggest influence on you since you started on this course?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know really. [name] – who’s my best friend, has had more influence than anyone else. Might be because I might go slightly insane if he wasn’t there. But, I don’t know. 

Interviewer:	Does he motivate you and things like that?

Subject:	He does the opposite. But it means I’m having to motivate him, which sort of – I can’t make – badger him to do work if I haven’t done it myself. So I end up having to make myself do work as well. If that makes any sense at all.

Interviewer:	Yeah, (lost words) do you think you generally support each other?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had to do much group work on your course?

Subject:	We haven’t had to do that much of it, but when we do it does my head in. I don’t – it – I don’t mind doing group work, with other people (yeah) in theory but in practice it’s just the hassle of trying to arrange meetings and you never feel that you’ve actually done anything because this – in like a normal project you know, you do the whole thing from start to finish, and in group things you do little random tasks and you never really seem to have done that much at all, it just kind of happens.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the advantages of doing group work?

Subject:	I don’t really think there’s many advantages at all. I just – I prefer doing it on my own.

Interviewer:	Do you think that group work will help you when you do go into industry?

Subject:	Do what?

Interviewer:	Do you think that group work will help you when you do go into industry? The skills that you’ve got from it?

Subject:	It might do. I mean they are very much, ooooh team work, team work, which is fine, I can do team work and that’ll be – but I think you do – there is more actual sort of tasks, individual tasks to do, for on the whole – for the like good of the team as a whole, rather than sort of when you do sort of group work at uni, it’s just kind of well you do what you want to do but it’s – there’s no real things that you ought to be doing and never feels that you’ve got that much done.

Interviewer:	Like you haven’t really achieved anything? (yes) How do you choose who to work with, when you work in groups? Do you get put into groups or…?

Subject:	Yeah, we just get stuck in them. At the moment we’re doing a tin can project and we just get stuck in groups for that. 

Interviewer:	Do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn’t that bother you?

Subject:	Erm, generally I work in – well, just the way the course is I think I’m working with men more anyway. But I do quite like it if I’m working with one of the girls as well.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is?

Subject:	We have a different – a different relationship with females than we do with males. But having said that, as long as I’ve got my core group of female friends, I couldn’t really give a monkeys about having any others. Just sort of random acquaintance females – I’m not that bothered about…

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any examples of like good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	It was just – oh, a whole module on a garden sprinkler, in a group – and you had to. And we had erm a – he was doing ergonomics, but he’d actually already done a degree in automotive, so he kind of made himself our little team captain, and then we just did what he said. And it turned out OK, in the finish. I mean I did what I was told to do and that was it. It was OK. Well, we didn’t do brilliantly but we did alright. We got 64 or something, so that’s OK.

Interviewer:	Did you feel he took charge because you were a woman or because of him, really?

Subject:	Because he was older. It wasn’t because I was a woman. He’d got other people in – he’d got other males in the group, and he was in charge of them just as much as he was me. 

Interviewer:	He thought he knew more than you?

Subject:	Yeah, well he did. He might not have known more about the actual subject, but I don’t know. I mean you do need someone who’s going to lead the group and I didn’t particularly want to, so …

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there’s any teaching or advice that you’ve had that will help you when you go on placement?

Subject:	Erm, not really?

Interviewer:	Or any skills that you’ve learnt?

Subject:	Erm, I guess erm writing lab reports but I don’t know if that’s the sort of detail I’ll be doing it. I think industry’s just a whole different ball game anyway. I don’t – I’m not really sure what to expect to be honest.

Interviewer:	Does that worry you at all?

Subject:	Not really, mainly because my best friend did a year in industry before she was at uni and she was a bit worried before she got there and the first sort of few weeks were a bit difficult settling in, but in the end it was the best thing she could ever have done. She like really got loads of confidence from doing it and said to me that she made really good friends there, so. And they don’t – I don’t assume that they’ll throw you in at the deep end, because at the end of the day, if you did it wrong, it’s more work for them to sort it out. They’ll just kind of break you in gently and show you what it is your supposed to be doing and not just leave you to your own before you know what you’re doing so.

Interviewer:	So do you think there is anything that the university could do to help you all prepare for being on placement?

Subject:	Er, I don’t really know because you don’t – if you’re on placement, you’re doing things that you don’t do at university.

Interviewer:	You said earlier that you feel like you’re learning for learning’s sake, do you think that what you’re doing at university should be geared more ... 

Subject:	Well at the moment it is – we do need to learn – it is (?) to learn it because it is the background to what it is that you will be doing. If you didn’t understand the stuff behind it then you wouldn’t really know what you were doing in industry. So you do kind of need to know it. It – it’s more just that the actual learning – the actual more kind of facts and stuff, kind of annoys me a bit sometimes. But if you can understand the principles and everything, without actually knowing – so it’s specifically (lost words) then this (? Words drowned out by noise) deal with structure.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that at this time now – you feel ready to go on placement now?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know whether I’m ready for my placement. I’m just I don’t want to do my – I don’t want to do my final year, next year. That is more how I’m viewing it. I want to do something different. And as well if – ‘cos you have to do a final year project, ‘cos if I’ve done some time working in industry, I’m hoping that would help – give me some connections maybe and just give me more of an idea how the industry does work, then I’ll be able to help – er maybe it will make it easier to do my project. If you want information out of people, you’ll know more how to get it.

Interviewer:	So you’re hoping that the industrial experience will help when you come back for your final year?

Subject:	Yeah. (Ok) Just gives me a bit of time away from exams, because you get a bit fed up of them when you’ve being doing them since you were 12. 

Interviewer:	Do you think there’s any other reasons that the work placement can be a good idea?

Subject:	Because I don’t really know what I want to do – because like our course is materials and management, I suppose, in theory, I could go and manage but – but I don’t know. You think when you’ve had a – when you’ve done the course that maybe – that maybe you should look at going into industry first and like I say, there’s loads of people at the moment doing actual management courses and (lost words) anyway. So I don’t know. I’m hoping it will give me more idea and I mean industry as well, its such as vague thing to say, because within materials I could go into copper bits or metals or ceramics or polymers, then within them you can go in like – there’s so many different branches, I’m hoping it’ll at least allow me to cross something off and it’ll mean I definitely don’t want to – give me some more idea of what it is that I actually do want to do because at the moment, I just don’t know.

Interviewer:	Ok, that makes sense.

Subject:	And the money will be useful as well.

Interviewer:	I take it you don’t know where you’re going to be going yet?

Subject:	At the moment, no and I’ve got interviews with [company] erm so I might be working for [company] at [town] and I’ve applied there for doing a metallurgic, like materials placement but it just said, at the interviews, a technical placement, so .. I’m (?) kind of doing like a general thing and then maybe actual – the physical materials might be later on, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	So, when you’ve been applying to companies what sort of things have you been looking at? What’s attracted you to the companies? Have you looked at things like money and the type of work that you’d be doing?

Subject:	Oh yeah, everything – as long as – I’ve just been applying for something – as long as it’s like materials related (yeah) and it’s within a location I wanted to be, I’ve not been that bothered because, at the end of the day, some experience is better than none.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so location’s been quite important?

Subject:	Yeah, I want to be able to get to [this university] relatively easily – just ‘cos that’s where my boyfriend is. I don’t want to move South, because it’s too expensive (yes).

Interviewer:	OK, have you done much research into the different companies that you’ve applied to?

Subject:	Erm, well I’ve looked at some stuff, but then I’ve just had a look on the web sites. Just had a look to get a general idea of what they are like. Erm, because, it’s only a year. As long as they’ve got a relatively good programme for you to do, it doesn’t really matter. You’re not necessarily going to go and work for them afterwards anyway. But [company] - I went to a – they came here and I went to like an evening thing where they told you about them, and [company] do seem to have a proper scheme and it does allow you to change and develop – that’s good. There’s a lot of companies that it’s a bit harder to see really what they’re offering as much but…

Interviewer:	Have you applied to smaller companies?

Subject:	Yeah, I’ve applied to a few. Well, you think they’re smaller, but actually when you look on the web sites, they’re like oh actually they’re really big – but they’re ones that nobody’s particularly heard of. They’re not the ones that come to the Careers day, they’re like really – they are proper global corporation things so, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Have you got a preference which type of company you’d like to work for?

Subject:	I really don’t mind, I just want something.

Interviewer:	Have the university been very involved in helping you find something?

Subject:	No. Erm, you’re pretty much left to your own devices. You get – [placement co-ordinator] sends out emails when companies say that they’ve got student placements, they send them to us so we can look at them, and its like, I went to the careers service myself, just ‘cos I was in a bit of a stress, but by the time I got there I’d already sorted things out anyway, and she just like had a quick look at my CV and my covering letter and that sort of thing, then generally reassured me that I was doing ok, and if – ‘cos I was saying I might just have a random year doing something random because I just really don’t fancy starting my final year. But then, if it’s too random it might just put me out of the mood altogether, and stop me coming back and finishing it and then it’s a waste of 2 years of my life.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university should be more involved in helping you find a placement …?

Subject:	Well, at the moment, there’s not really that much they can do, because at the end of the day, you’ve got to write your own application forms. They can’t do it for you erm there’s not really that much they can do anyway.

Interviewer:	Would you say that was very good – if you had a list of companies and things like that, or do you have to go out and find the companies – the (?) yourself?

Subject:	No, she’s got – I don’t know, she might just have – you know it maybe contacts that she’s built up and things, and she emails you those. There are actual, you know, I’ve got jobs and then you can apply for them. I mean a lot – in the beginning, they (student is yawning and her words can’t be heard) so there’s quite a few (?) companies that (lost words).

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the best and the worst thing about going on placement?

Subject:	The work will – it’ll just be the fact that it’s going to be 9-5 everyday. But, at least you’ve got your weekends again. You don’t have anything hanging over your head can go home every weekend and it’ll just – it’ll be nice to just be in a completely different environment and just the fact that everything’s gonna be new. It’ll be learning about the whole different way of – how it all works and meeting different people earning some money, and being one step closer to actually being independent. Because at the minute you kind of play at being independent because well, I’m – I’m probably am more than the other people, because my parents just – they stick the money in the bank for me, for my rent and everything else so I get all the freedom without any of the responsibilities. So, next year if I’m on placement, I’ll have to be doing it all myself.

Interviewer:	Are you looking forward to all that then?

Subject:	It’s kind of scary actually, but then I know my parents are always there anyway, if it all goes horribly wrong. So it probably helps, but it will be interesting to try and be a proper adult.

Interviewer:	Do you think what’s expected of you and how you’ll be treated will be different?

Interviewer:	In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Go travelling for, I don’t know, a year at the most, but I’d probably do a bit less.

Interviewer:	Would you like a job that involves travel?

Subject:	Yeah, I wouldn’t mind working in different countries actually. In fact I might even just do that and not actually travel and just sort of have little sort of holidays – proper travel travelling. Interviewer:	Erm, what would be the ideal career, do you think?

Subject:	Well, I think it’ll have to have people in it somewhere because I generally like being around people, a lot of the time. I couldn’t – I couldn’t just be in an office but by the same token I wouldn’t just want to be, you know, going round all the time because although it might be different sites, they’re gonna be essentially the same. I fancy getting – you know – a relatively good job by the end of it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are barriers to trying to get those things in a career?

Subject:	I don’t know. I don’t suppose it’ll be any different to anybody else, ‘cos as long as you put the work in you usually get what you want at the end of it, don’t you?

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that if you do go into the industry, that the career prospects are good?

Subject:	I think, well unless I’ve been lied to, they’re supposed to be fairly good. ‘Cos there’s still like – there’s a lot of things still going on, it’s not like some industries that’ve kind of come to a standstill. There’s a lot going on in design and technology and that’s a plus as well. It’s all different things – ‘cos like the ceramics guy – I really like [name] actually – and he was saying like what he’s doing it at the moment, in his research. So I don’t know – there’s things happening so you’d assume that it will be alright.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the decisions that you’ve made about your career so far? Would you do it differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	Erm, well if I was a gonna do it again, I would do something different just because I’ve already done this one, but yeah, I know what you mean though. Interviewer:	So you don’t regret doing the course that you’ve done?

Subject:	Not really. I mean it’s – as far as course go it’s alright – it has it’s moments of utter boredom but then at other times it’s pretty good, so.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students, like in Social sciences or Humanities?

Subject:	Yeah, in – because a lot of ours is still like being in school a lot of the time. Interviewer:	Would you have liked to be on a course that is more just lectures?

Subject:	No. If it was just management it would drive me nutty, because there are no right answers and for a change I like it – it’s quite stimulating to argue your way round in circles, but if that was it – just my course, just writing essays, going round in circles, using everyone else’s different points of view, arguing with each other, I’d go nutty. Subject:	 (long pause) I really don’t know.

Interviewer:	Would you say that it’s masculine?

Subject:	I’ve got the word closed – I’m thinking.

Interviewer:	Why are you thinking of that?

Subject:	Well, because there’s not that much information about it, so you have to go looking for it if you want it.

Subject:	Erm, not really. They maybe could do a bit more to promote it earlier on. But since I’ve been looking for a placement and that, (at that age?), if you go to the careers fairs, there are the big players there, so. It probably is masculine dominated, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is masculine, purely because of the numbers of men in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’ll stay like that or get better?

Subject:	I think it’ll, it’ll have to become more feminine, if more women join it, but I guess a lot – you’re not going be a girly twirly girl if you’re going into engineering.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the fact it is so masculine and closed will cause you any problems if you do decide to go into the industry?

Subject:	No, because they do actually – whether they really want them, or if they secretly don’t, just for like appearances sake they do need some women in the industry.

Interviewer:	What about when you try and develop your career and get promoted and things like that? Do you think it’ll be OK then?

Subject:	Yeah, if I’m the best then one would assume that they’d promote me, if I’m not the best, then fair dos - if I make the effort ...

I don’t – it – I don’t mind doing group work, with other people (yeah) in theory but in practice it’s just the hassle of trying to arrange meetings and you never feel that you’ve actually done anything because this – in like a normal project you know, you do the whole thing from start to finish, and in group things you do little random tasks and you never really seem to have done that much at all, it just kind of happens.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the advantages of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really think there’s many advantages at all. I just – I prefer doing it on my own.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that group work will help you when you do go into industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Do what?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that group work will help you when you do go into industry? The skills that you’ve got from it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It might do. I mean they are very much, ooooh team work, team work, which is fine, I can do team work and that’ll be – but I think you do – there is more actual sort of tasks, individual tasks to do, for on the whole – for the like good of the team as a whole, rather than sort of when you do sort of group work at uni, it’s just kind of well you do what you want to do but it’s – there’s no real things that you ought to be doing and never feels that you’ve got that much done.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like you haven’t really achieved anything? (yes) How do you choose who to work with, when you work in groups? Do you get put into groups or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we just get stuck in them. At the moment we’re doing a tin can project and we just get stuck in groups for that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn’t that bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, generally I work in – well, just the way the course is I think I’m working with men more anyway. But I do quite like it if I’m working with one of the girls as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We have a different – a different relationship with females than we do with males. But having said that, as long as I’ve got my core group of female friends, I couldn’t really give a monkeys about having any others. Just sort of random acquaintance females – I’m not that bothered about…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got any examples of like good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was just – oh, a whole module on a garden sprinkler, in a group – and you had to. And we had erm a – he was doing ergonomics, but he’d actually already done a degree in automotive, so he kind of made himself our little team captain, and then we just did what he said. And it turned out OK, in the finish. I mean I did what I was told to do and that was it. It was OK. Well, we didn’t do brilliantly but we did alright. We got 64 or something, so that’s OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you feel he took charge because you were a woman or because of him, really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because he was older. It wasn’t because I was a woman. He’d got other people in – he’d got other males in the group, and he was in charge of them just as much as he was me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: He thought he knew more than you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, well he did. He might not have known more about the actual subject, but I don’t know. I mean you do need someone who’s going to lead the group and I didn’t particularly want to, so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there’s any teaching or advice that you’ve had that will help you when you go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or any skills that you’ve learnt?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I guess erm writing lab reports but I don’t know if that’s the sort of detail I’ll be doing it. I think industry’s just a whole different ball game anyway. I don’t – I’m not really sure what to expect to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that worry you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, mainly because my best friend did a year in industry before she was at uni and she was a bit worried before she got there and the first sort of few weeks were a bit difficult settling in, but in the end it was the best thing she could ever have done. She like really got loads of confidence from doing it and said to me that she made really good friends there, so. And they don’t – I don’t assume that they’ll throw you in at the deep end, because at the end of the day, if you did it wrong, it’s more work for them to sort it out. They’ll just kind of break you in gently and show you what it is your supposed to be doing and not just leave you to your own before you know what you’re doing so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think there is anything that the university could do to help you all prepare for being on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t really know because you don’t – if you’re on placement, you’re doing things that you don’t do at university.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said earlier that you feel like you’re learning for learning’s sake, do you think that what you’re doing at university should be geared more ...

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well at the moment it is – we do need to learn – it is (?) to learn it because it is the background to what it is that you will be doing. If you didn’t understand the stuff behind it then you wouldn’t really know what you were doing in industry. So you do kind of need to know it. It – it’s more just that the actual learning – the actual more kind of facts and stuff, kind of annoys me a bit sometimes. But if you can understand the principles and everything, without actually knowing – so it’s specifically (lost words) then this (? Words drowned out by noise) deal with structure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that at this time now – you feel ready to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know whether I’m ready for my placement. I’m just I don’t want to do my – I don’t want to do my final year, next year. That is more how I’m viewing it. I want to do something different. And as well if – ‘cos you have to do a final year project, ‘cos if I’ve done some time working in industry, I’m hoping that would help – give me some connections maybe and just give me more of an idea how the industry does work, then I’ll be able to help – er maybe it will make it easier to do my project. If you want information out of people, you’ll know more how to get it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re hoping that the industrial experience will help when you come back for your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. (Ok) Just gives me a bit of time away from exams, because you get a bit fed up of them when you’ve being doing them since you were 12.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there’s any other reasons that the work placement can be a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because I don’t really know what I want to do – because like our course is materials and management, I suppose, in theory, I could go and manage but – but I don’t know. You think when you’ve had a – when you’ve done the course that maybe – that maybe you should look at going into industry first and like I say, there’s loads of people at the moment doing actual management courses and (lost words) anyway. So I don’t know. I’m hoping it will give me more idea and I mean industry as well, its such as vague thing to say, because within materials I could go into copper bits or metals or ceramics or polymers, then within them you can go in like – there’s so many different branches, I’m hoping it’ll at least allow me to cross something off and it’ll mean I definitely don’t want to – give me some more idea of what it is that I actually do want to do because at the moment, I just don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that makes sense.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And the money will be useful as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I take it you don’t know where you’re going to be going yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At the moment, no and I’ve got interviews with [company] erm so I might be working for [company] at [town] and I’ve applied there for doing a metallurgic, like materials placement but it just said, at the interviews, a technical placement, so .. I’m (?) kind of doing like a general thing and then maybe actual – the physical materials might be later on, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, when you’ve been applying to companies what sort of things have you been looking at? What’s attracted you to the companies? Have you looked at things like money and the type of work that you’d be doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah, everything – as long as – I’ve just been applying for something – as long as it’s like materials related (yeah) and it’s within a location I wanted to be, I’ve not been that bothered because, at the end of the day, some experience is better than none.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so location’s been quite important?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I want to be able to get to [this university] relatively easily – just ‘cos that’s where my boyfriend is. I don’t want to move South, because it’s too expensive (yes).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you done much research into the different companies that you’ve applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I’ve looked at some stuff, but then I’ve just had a look on the web sites. Just had a look to get a general idea of what they are like. Erm, because, it’s only a year. As long as they’ve got a relatively good programme for you to do, it doesn’t really matter. You’re not necessarily going to go and work for them afterwards anyway. But [company] - I went to a – they came here and I went to like an evening thing where they told you about them, and [company] do seem to have a proper scheme and it does allow you to change and develop – that’s good. There’s a lot of companies that it’s a bit harder to see really what they’re offering as much but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you applied to smaller companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’ve applied to a few. Well, you think they’re smaller, but actually when you look on the web sites, they’re like oh actually they’re really big – but they’re ones that nobody’s particularly heard of. They’re not the ones that come to the Careers day, they’re like really – they are proper global corporation things so, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a preference which type of company you’d like to work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I really don’t mind, I just want something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have the university been very involved in helping you find something?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Erm, you’re pretty much left to your own devices. You get – [placement co-ordinator] sends out emails when companies say that they’ve got student placements, they send them to us so we can look at them, and its like, I went to the careers service myself, just ‘cos I was in a bit of a stress, but by the time I got there I’d already sorted things out anyway, and she just like had a quick look at my CV and my covering letter and that sort of thing, then generally reassured me that I was doing ok, and if – ‘cos I was saying I might just have a random year doing something random because I just really don’t fancy starting my final year. But then, if it’s too random it might just put me out of the mood altogether, and stop me coming back and finishing it and then it’s a waste of 2 years of my life.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university should be more involved in helping you find a placement …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, at the moment, there’s not really that much they can do, because at the end of the day, you’ve got to write your own application forms. They can’t do it for you erm there’s not really that much they can do anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you say that was very good – if you had a list of companies and things like that, or do you have to go out and find the companies – the (?) yourself?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, she’s got – I don’t know, she might just have – you know it maybe contacts that she’s built up and things, and she emails you those. There are actual, you know, I’ve got jobs and then you can apply for them. I mean a lot – in the beginning, they (student is yawning and her words can’t be heard) so there’s quite a few (?) companies that (lost words).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be the best and the worst thing about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The work will – it’ll just be the fact that it’s going to be 9-5 everyday. But, at least you’ve got your weekends again. You don’t have anything hanging over your head can go home every weekend and it’ll just – it’ll be nice to just be in a completely different environment and just the fact that everything’s gonna be new. It’ll be learning about the whole different way of – how it all works and meeting different people earning some money, and being one step closer to actually being independent. Because at the minute you kind of play at being independent because well, I’m – I’m probably am more than the other people, because my parents just – they stick the money in the bank for me, for my rent and everything else so I get all the freedom without any of the responsibilities. So, next year if I’m on placement, I’ll have to be doing it all myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you looking forward to all that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s kind of scary actually, but then I know my parents are always there anyway, if it all goes horribly wrong. So it probably helps, but it will be interesting to try and be a proper adult.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Will you still be living in [university town] hopefully or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it depends. I don’t really know. I’m not that – I’m not that bothered if I’m actually living in [town] because – [town] (lost words) chips – as long as I’m like within distance, so I can like visit (yeah) then that’s OK. Cos if it was at [town], then it would be a bit of a commute to go to – travelling [university town] to [town] every day, but it’s – so I’d just live in [town], I expect. Especially, with [company] being a big company, I think they’d have quite a few different placement students anyway. Well, I think that’s how it works. From other people I’ve spoken to, who are on the engineering, at the moment they tend to be like a group of you, and you just live together, although that might do your head in, if you’re living and working together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that work will be different from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because, you’ll be actually doing something. Quite what, I’m not sure, but even if it’s completely routine tasks, it’s an actual practical something. It’s not sitting and writing notes and leaving and going home. It’s not learning, like that. It’s not studying it’s something else – quite what I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think what’s expected of you and how you’ll be treated will be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well yeah because they’re gonna expect you to be being productive in some way or other. I’m not quite sure how they’re gonna treat you. I assume they’ll treat you like any other employee - whereby if you do what you’re supposed to be doing, then everyone’s happy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I really don’t know. I could be, you know, in a little lab somewhere breaking things. Er, I don’t know, I could be travelling by then. One of my cunning plans is that I can, if I do my year in industry, decide what it is I do want to do - do my final year, finish university, get a job in whatever it is I’ve decided I want to do it in, in one of these graduate scheme things, which are usually about 2 years. Once I’ve finished all the training, and earned some money along the way, say right, I’m going to go travelling now. Go travelling for, I don’t know, a year at the most, but I’d probably do a bit less.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like a job that involves travel?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I wouldn’t mind working in different countries actually. In fact I might even just do that and not actually travel and just sort of have little sort of holidays – proper travel travelling. But yeah, the cunning plan was that we’re then travelling a bit, because once you’ve got the training, then, they’re more likely to say, well you know, we’ve invested all this money in you, then we’ll have you back sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Erm, what would be the ideal career, do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I think it’ll have to have people in it somewhere because I generally like being around people, a lot of the time. Erm, I’m not very sure doing what – I wouldn’t just want to be – I don’t – it needs to be a job that’s got a lot of variety in it. I couldn’t do the same thing every day. I couldn’t – I couldn’t just be in an office but by the same token I wouldn’t just want to be, you know, going round all the time because although it might be different sites, they’re gonna be essentially the same. So, whatever it is it needs to be fairly varied. (Yeah) And not something where you get stuck. It has to be something where I could like, progress a lot. I fancy getting – you know – a relatively good job by the end of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are barriers to trying to get those things in a career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I don’t suppose it’ll be any different to anybody else, ‘cos as long as you put the work in you usually get what you want at the end of it, don’t you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that if you do go into the industry, that the career prospects are good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think, well unless I’ve been lied to, they’re supposed to be fairly good. ‘Cos there’s still like – there’s a lot of things still going on, it’s not like some industries that’ve kind of come to a standstill. There’s a lot going on in design and technology and that’s a plus as well. It’s all different things – ‘cos like the ceramics guy – I really like [name] actually – and he was saying like what he’s doing it at the moment, in his research. So I don’t know – there’s things happening so you’d assume that it will be alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the decisions that you’ve made about your career so far? Would you do it differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well if I was a gonna do it again, I would do something different just because I’ve already done this one, but yeah, I know what you mean though. I would – I don’t think I would necessarily change – I probably would’ve done chemistry instead of materials eng – well no, I would’ve done geology but I don’t what jobs are like at the end of geology, and I really like geology because I had an absolutely brilliant teacher at ‘A’ level, and I could have come to uni, and had y’know lecturers that didn’t inspire me and I would have been just as bored there anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you don’t regret doing the course that you’ve done?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. I mean it’s – as far as course go it’s alright – it has it’s moments of utter boredom but then at other times it’s pretty good, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your educational experiences differ from other students, like in Social sciences or Humanities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, in – because a lot of ours is still like being in school a lot of the time. Especially, in first year, with having such a small group, it was sitting in a classroom and being taught, and you could ask questions, whereas a lot of the social sciences – they’re such huge groups that are just in a lecture theatre and there’s no contact involved between the lecturer and he’s just – my business modules were like that. Well, actually, I used to talk – (that was the difference between the rest of the engineers?) - they all hated it – what was it? - marketing and management of human resources and they were like we’re all engineers, why do we have to be? But I quite liked it, obviously, choosing to have done management anyway. You know, so they’d all just laugh when I used to answer questions and got involved – I quite liked it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you have liked to be on a course that is more just lectures?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. If it was just management it would drive me nutty, because there are no right answers and for a change I like it – it’s quite stimulating to argue your way round in circles, but if that was it – just my course, just writing essays, going round in circles, using everyone else’s different points of view, arguing with each other, I’d go nutty. It’s nice – at least in engineering, you know that answers are right or wrong you can’t be – well, it could be if you listen to this person but maybe not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics or the culture of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (long pause) I really don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you say that it’s masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve got the word closed – I’m thinking.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why are you thinking of that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, because there’s not that much information about it, so you have to go looking for it if you want it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think it’s like that? … Do you think it should be like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. They maybe could do a bit more to promote it earlier on. But since I’ve been looking for a placement and that, (at that age?), if you go to the careers fairs, there are the big players there, so. It probably is masculine dominated, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is masculine, purely because of the numbers of men in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’ll stay like that or get better?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’ll, it’ll have to become more feminine, if more women join it, but I guess a lot – you’re not going be a girly twirly girl if you’re going into engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the fact it is so masculine and closed will cause you any problems if you do decide to go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because they do actually – whether they really want them, or if they secretly don’t, just for like appearances sake they do need some women in the industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about when you try and develop your career and get promoted and things like that? Do you think it’ll be OK then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, if I’m the best then one would assume that they’d promote me, if I’m not the best, then fair dos - if I make the effort ...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s in then, thank you very much.
